mean: to accept something as true without checking it
ex: Don't assume the Harbour line is running late just because it rained last night; check the app first.
note: Assume = believe without proof. 'Assume charge' (common in Indian news) means take up a post: 'She assumed charge as collector.'
ex2: Never assume a fast bowler is tired in his last over; the best ones save their quickest ball for the end.

mean: to decide something is true after thinking about the facts
ex: After checking the meter twice, the electrician could only conclude that the wiring in the old Kolkata flat was faulty.
note: Also means 'to end': 'The meeting concluded at six.' The noun is 'conclusion'; 'jump to conclusions' means decide too fast.
ex2: Doctors cannot conclude anything from one blood test, so Sameer has to repeat it next week at the AIIMS lab.

mean: facts or signs that show whether something is true
ex: The CCTV footage was the only evidence that the scooter had been parked outside the chemist's shop in Lucknow.
note: Uncountable: say 'a piece of evidence' or 'a lot of evidence', never 'an evidence' or 'evidences'.
ex2: There is little evidence that sipping hot water every hour cures a cold, whatever the family WhatsApp group says.

mean: following clear, sensible reasoning
ex: Shifting the wedding to December was the logical choice, since the monsoon would ruin an outdoor mandap in July.
note: Opposite: illogical. 'Logical' is about the reasoning being sound, not about being clever or unemotional.
ex2: For a farmer in Vidarbha with very little rain, switching from sugarcane to millets is the logical step.

mean: connected to what is being discussed or done
ex: The interviewer in the Bengaluru office said Arjun's experience as a college cricket captain was relevant to the team-lead role.
note: Often misspelled 'relavant'. The opposite is 'irrelevant', not 'unrelevant'.
ex2: At the panchayat meeting, the sarpanch asked everyone to raise only issues relevant to the new water pipeline.

mean: to study something closely, part by part, to understand it
ex: The coach asked Shreyas to analyse the video of every ball he got out to this season.
note: British/Indian spelling is 'analyse'; American is 'analyze'. Noun: analysis, plural analyses.
ex2: Every Sunday, students at the Kota coaching centre sit down to analyse the mistakes in their mock tests.

mean: to work something out from the clues you have
ex: From the half-eaten paratha and the open window, Amma could infer that the neighbour's cat had visited the kitchen.
note: The speaker implies (hints); the listener infers (works it out). 'Are you inferring I'm lazy?' is wrong; say 'implying'.
ex2: From Coach Bhatia's silence after the match, the players could infer that he was unhappy with their fielding.

mean: an unfair leaning for or against someone or something
ex: Fans accused the umpire of bias after three close lbw calls all went against the visiting team.
note: The adjective is 'biased': 'a biased report', not 'a bias report'. Confirmation bias = noticing only what supports what you already believe.
ex2: The Hyderabad firm now hides candidates' names from interviewers to reduce bias against women and small-town applicants.

mean: the situation or surrounding facts that explain something
ex: Taken out of context, Chachaji's joke in the family WhatsApp group sounded far ruder than he meant it.
note: 'Quoted out of context' is a common trick: a line cut from what came before it can seem to mean the opposite.
ex2: Without the context of the 1991 reforms, the textbook chapter on India's economy makes little sense to Class 12 students.

mean: a particular way of seeing or thinking about something
ex: A week on her uncle's farm in Punjab gave Simran a new perspective on why vegetable prices jump.
note: 'Put things in perspective' means judging how important something really is, without exaggerating it.
ex2: Working night shifts at the district hospital gave Dr Thomas a fresh perspective on how tired the nurses really are.

mean: a likely result, or something suggested without being said directly
ex: Nobody at the Pune startup had thought through the implication of storing customer data on a free server abroad.
note: Often plural for effects: 'the implications of the new rule'. Linked to 'imply', not to 'implicate' (show someone is involved in a crime).
ex2: The implication of the captain's remark was clear: Rahul would not open the batting in the next match.

mean: based on facts, not on personal feelings or opinions
ex: The editor told the new reporter to stay objective while covering the dispute between the two housing societies.
note: Opposite: subjective. As a noun, 'objective' means a goal: 'the objective of this meeting'.
ex2: It is hard to stay objective when you are judging a rangoli contest that your own daughter has entered.

mean: an idea you accept as true and build an argument or plan on
ex: The whole plan rested on the premise that the new metro line would open before Diwali, and it didn't.
note: Don't mix with 'premises', which means a building and its land: 'No smoking on the premises.'
ex2: The film's premise is simple: a dabbawala delivers the wrong tiffin, and two strangers start writing to each other.

mean: a small but important difference in meaning or feeling
ex: Good translators catch every nuance of a Ghalib couplet.
note: A 'nuanced view' sees more than one side of a question.
ex2: The new HR manager in Gurugram missed the nuance when her team said the deadline was 'a bit tight'.

mean: seeming likely to be true or reasonable
ex: Rohan's excuse that the Delhi metro was stuck in a tunnel for an hour sounded plausible, so the teacher let him in.
note: Plausible is not the same as true: it only seems likely. Good liars tell very plausible stories.
ex2: The police found the truck driver's story plausible: a stray cow had run onto the highway near Nashik.

mean: clear, with all its parts fitting together sensibly
ex: After two sleepless nights before the board exam, Ananya could barely write a coherent answer.
note: Opposite: incoherent. 'Coherent' is about ideas fitting together; 'cohesive' is about a group sticking together.
ex2: After months of chasing every new idea, the two founders finally had a coherent plan for their food startup.

mean: a link where two things tend to rise or fall together
ex: The study found a correlation between ice-cream sales and drownings in Goa, but summer heat was driving both.
note: Correlation is not causation: two things moving together does not prove one causes the other.
ex2: Teachers in Jaipur noticed a correlation between late-night phone use and sleepy students in the first period.

mean: a common belief or step in reasoning that is wrong
ex: It is a fallacy that a student who scores low in the Class 10 boards cannot do well in life.
note: In logic, a fallacy is a faulty step in an argument (like a straw man), even if the conclusion happens to be true.
ex2: It is a fallacy that a costlier wedding means a happier marriage, though many families still spend as if it were true.

mean: an idea that might explain something, which still has to be tested
ex: Dr Iyer's hypothesis was that the dengue cases came from water lying in the construction site's open tanks.
note: Plural: hypotheses (high-POTH-uh-seez). A hypothesis is still to be tested; a scientific theory has been tested many times.
ex2: The captain's hypothesis was that the Chennai pitch would turn after lunch, so he picked three spinners.

mean: very careful and strict, checking every detail
ex: Every new medicine must pass rigorous trials before doctors at a Chennai hospital can prescribe it.
note: Don't confuse with 'vigorous' (full of energy). A rigorous check is exact; a vigorous one is energetic.
ex2: Before the new bridge in Guwahati opened, engineers ran rigorous load tests with fully loaded trucks.

mean: based on what is seen or tested, not only on theory
ex: To check the farmers' belief that neem spray protects cotton, the agriculture college in Nagpur collected empirical data from fifty fields.
note: Opposite: theoretical. 'Empirical evidence' means evidence from observation or experiment, not from argument alone.
ex2: Kabir's grandmother trusts experience, but he wants empirical proof that turmeric milk really cures a cough.

mean: something that seems impossible or self-contradicting but may still be true
ex: It is a paradox that Cherrapunji, one of the wettest places on earth, runs short of drinking water in winter.
note: 'Paradoxically' is a useful sentence opener: 'Paradoxically, building more roads can create more traffic.'
ex2: Here is the paradox of the Mumbai local: it is unbearably crowded, yet it is still the fastest way home.

mean: a sharp split between two opposite things or ideas
ex: The TV panel fell into a false dichotomy: either build the highway or save the forest, with nothing in between.
note: A 'false dichotomy' pretends only two options exist. Don't use 'dichotomy' just to mean any 'difference'.
ex2: Many parents see a dichotomy between sports and studies, but Smriti topped her class and played state-level hockey.

mean: a simple rule of thumb that helps you decide quickly
ex: Nani's heuristic for buying mangoes at Crawford Market was simple: smell the stalk end before you pay.
note: Heuristics save time but can mislead; many biases are heuristics gone wrong. Also an adjective: 'a heuristic approach'.
ex2: A useful heuristic in any entrance exam is to skip a question that takes more than two minutes and come back later.

mean: saying the same thing twice in different words, adding nothing
ex: The Hyderabad ad agency dropped the slogan 'new innovation' after the client pointed out the tautology.
note: Common slips: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'PIN number', 'free gift'. Just say 'return', 'repeat', 'PIN', 'gift'.
ex2: The 'free gift' promised on the sweet-shop banner in Indore is a tautology, since every gift is free.

mean: to think carefully about something before you decide
ex: Before you accept the job in Dubai, consider how much you will miss your parents back in Patna.
ex2: The selectors will consider young players from the Ranji Trophy for the tour of Australia.
note: No 'about' after it: say 'consider the offer', not 'consider about the offer'. 'Consider him honest' means think he is honest.

mean: to suddenly understand or become aware of something
ex: It took Arjun one week in the hostel to realise how much work his mother did at home.
ex2: Fans did not realise how good the young spinner was until he took five wickets at Eden Gardens.
note: Use 'realise' for what you understand yourself. For news someone told you, say 'found out' or 'learnt', not 'realised' or 'came to know'.

mean: fair and sensible; based on good thinking
ex: Asking the landlord to fix the leaking roof before the monsoon is a perfectly reasonable request.
ex2: The auto driver in Kochi asked for a reasonable fare without any haggling, so Neha gave him a tip.
note: A 'reasonable price' is fair, not necessarily cheap. 'Beyond reasonable doubt' is the test a court uses before it finds someone guilty.

mean: to judge how good, useful or correct something is
ex: The school invited three teachers from outside to evaluate the science projects of Classes 6 to 8.
ex2: Before buying a second-hand bike in Ludhiana, Harjeet asked a mechanic to evaluate its engine.
note: Close to 'assess'. Don't add 'about': 'evaluate the plan', not 'evaluate about the plan'. Noun: evaluation.

mean: to reach an answer step by step from the facts you have
ex: Like Byomkesh Bakshi, little Tara tried to deduce from the crumbs on the stairs who had stolen the cake.
ex2: By noting which days the power went off, the residents could deduce that the cuts followed the factory shifts.
note: Close to 'infer'; 'deduce' suggests careful step-by-step logic, like a detective. Noun: deduction.

mean: to decide what something means, or explain its meaning
ex: Two teachers can interpret the same Kabir doha in completely different ways.
ex2: Sanjay chose to interpret his boss's silence on the leave request as a yes, and booked the Goa trip.
note: There is no word 'interpretate'. An interpreter translates speech aloud, for example in a court or at a summit.

mean: a clear, deep understanding of a person or situation
ex: The old fisherman's insight into the sea's moods saved the boat when the storm arrived early off Puri.
ex2: A month of working at a highway dhaba gave the young chef real insight into cooking for hundreds.
note: Say 'insight into', not 'insight on' or 'insight about'. 'Insightful' describes a remark or person showing it.

mean: to look at something very carefully to find mistakes or facts
ex: Auditors arrived from Mumbai to scrutinise the cooperative bank's loan records line by line.
ex2: Before the wedding, Bua would scrutinise every sweet box to make sure the laddoos came from the right shop.
note: Noun: scrutiny, as in 'under scrutiny'. Spelt with -ise in British and Indian English.

mean: the reasons behind a decision or plan
ex: The principal explained the rationale for the new rule: phones in class were causing too many fights.
ex2: Nobody in the cricket club understood the rationale behind dropping their best fielder for the final.
note: Stress the end: rash-uh-NAHL. Don't confuse it with 'rational', the adjective meaning sensible.

mean: something unusual that does not fit the normal pattern
ex: A spike in electricity use at 3 a.m. was the anomaly that led the engineer to an illegal connection.
ex2: Snow in that valley of Himachal in late April was an anomaly, and apple farmers worried about their crop.
note: Plural: anomalies. Adjective: anomalous, as in an anomalous result in a lab test.

mean: to notice or understand something that is not easy to see
ex: Through the thick Delhi smog, the driver could barely discern the outline of the toll plaza.
ex2: A good judge on a singing show can discern real talent from mere stage confidence.
note: Rather formal. 'A discerning buyer' is one with good judgement about quality.

mean: to guess what will happen from facts you already have
ex: You cannot extrapolate from one wet June that the whole monsoon will be heavy.
ex2: Using last year's sales, the Surat textile trader tried to extrapolate how many sarees he would sell this Diwali.
note: Use 'from': extrapolate from a small sample. It goes beyond the data, so it can mislead.

mean: to wrongly treat two different things as if they were the same
ex: Many people conflate being popular on Instagram with being good at business.
ex2: The new reporter tended to conflate the city municipal corporation with the state government.
note: Pattern: conflate A with B. More formal than 'mix up'; common in editorials and essays.

mean: false or fake, though it may look real
ex: The link between the opener's lucky socks and his centuries is a spurious one.
ex2: Fact-checkers traced the spurious quote to a parody account, not to the famous scientist.
note: Spurious = false or fake; specious = sounds right but is wrong. 'Spurious liquor' in Indian news means illegal, often deadly alcohol.

mean: noticing only the facts that support what you already believe
ex: Confirmation bias made Deepak share every news clip that agreed with him and ignore all the others.
ex2: Mrs Kulkarni is sure Tuesdays are unlucky, and confirmation bias makes her remember only the bad Tuesdays.
instead: seeing what you want to see
note: An idea from psychology. It explains why people enjoy groups and channels that only agree with them.

mean: the uneasy feeling when your actions and beliefs do not match
ex: A doctor who smokes lives with cognitive dissonance, knowing exactly what each cigarette does to his lungs.
ex2: Ravi felt cognitive dissonance every time he lectured his kids about plastic and then took five bags from the sabziwala.
note: From psychology. People often ease it with excuses like 'one won't hurt'. It is not the same as simple confusion.
